records.explanation: The statutory de novo action with joined injunction is limited to comprehensive-plan consistency challenges, absent a qualifying local opt-in. It does not establish that every separate construction injunction is proper. The rubric's categorical certiorari-only rule is wrong; its injunction penalty should be assessed against the claim's actual statutory or equitable basis.

first_intent.explanation: Criterion #12 (10 points) requires stating that certiorari under s. 163.3215(4) is the exclusive method of challenging a development order. The statute makes certiorari exclusive only where the local government has opted in by ordinance, and otherwise s. 163.3215(3) gives a de novo action that can carry injunctive relief. A model stating the statute accurately may lose the criterion. Penalty #14 (minus 15) penalizes saying petitioners may bring a separate injunction action, a statement s. 163.3215(3) can support for development-order consistency challenges. No instruction or criterion asks the model to identify or correct this citation.

No instruction or criterion asks the model to evaluate the Smith article. Criterion #19 awards 5 points for presenting county self-zoning immunity as an available position, and the rubric's support is this article plus Parkway Towers. The article accurately reports A1A, a county sewage plant case closely analogous here, and the 3d DCA's Parkway Towers holding, so the option is not baseless as a historical matter. But the article's own conclusion reads the law as having moved away from categorical immunity. The Supreme Court's Parkway Towers per curiam states a prospective expectation that zoning be changed first. Lee County in fact applied for and obtained this rezoning, and the 3d DCA's rule turns on whether the county's own ordinance waived the privilege, which nobody has checked against the Lee County LDC. The criterion therefore rewards a contestable argument presented without its contrary authority. A memo that flags it as weak or unavailable should not lose credit, and a grader should not treat it as settled law. I did not verify current Florida law as of January 1, 2025, including Temple Terrace's balancing test as applied to a county's own zoning or any express Lee County LDC self-application. The 1967 year is a separate bibliographic defect.

prior_intent.explanation: The full Smith article directly rejects unqualified county self-zoning immunity in its conclusion; its quoted A1A/Parkway account describes earlier doctrine. Criterion #19 rewards reliance on a historical passage against the source's own legal synthesis. Its PDF/repository year conflict is a separate bibliographic defect.

Prompts and rubrics treat §1606.2 as an operative Douglas-factor constraint on sworn MPD discipline. Official §1600.2(g) excludes sworn members. MPD’s own order may support factor analysis, but it is a different authority.

initial_intent.explanation: No instruction or criterion asks the model to notice that 6-B DCMR Chapter 16 excludes sworn MPD members (§ 1600.2(g)). The assignment 2 prompt directs the scope-of-review analysis 'under Douglas and D.C. Mun. Regs. tit. 6-B, § 1606.2 (2017)', and criterion 6 (4 points) rewards stating that § 1606.2 requires the deciding official to balance the Douglas-type factors, so a model that points out the regulation does not govern MPD sworn-member discipline does not earn that criterion. Criteria 4, 5 and 8 cite § 1606.2 only as part of the uploaded set.

records.explanation: Douglas explicitly requires agency proof of sanction-supporting facts, including consistency with other actions, in MSPB proceedings. A D.C. arbitral burden cannot be imported without another source, but the rubric treats the opposite as established by Douglas.

initial_intent.explanation: Criterion 4 (26 points) rewards stating that no uploaded authority requires MPD to prove the comparability of its comparator cases and cites Douglas at 305-06 among its sources. Douglas (5 MSPB 324, 333-34) puts on the agency the burden of proving the facts behind its penalty, expressly including consistency with other agency actions, so a model that reads Douglas that way and says so does not earn this criterion. Whether that MSPB-level allocation binds an arbitrator is arguable, but the criterion as written asserts an absence the uploaded opinion contradicts.

records.explanation: Douglas footnote 65 allows agency rebuttal after an appellant asserts disparity; it does not state a mandatory prima facie burden. The criterion should not reward an absolute rule in either direction.

initial_intent.explanation: Penalty criterion 5 (-18 points) penalizes stating that the employee must make an initial showing of disparate treatment before the agency bears a comparator burden, on the premise that this rule comes from outside the uploaded materials; its source list includes Douglas at 305-06. Douglas itself describes a raise-then-rebut sequence (5 MSPB 331 n.65; 334), so a model that draws that structure from the uploaded Douglas opinion can be penalized.
